clue.text: Cup of tea with 14

parts.note: cha is an old slang word for tea
the answer to 14 across is a swarm of pests, and lice are a classic example of one

explanation.surface: Someone orders a cup of tea to go with a cross-referenced item.
explanation.walkthrough: '14' points to the answer of 14 across, a swarm, which here stands for LICE, the creatures that typically make one.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalice is a goblet, especially a ceremonial drinking cup used in church.

clue.text: Singer knocking stuffing out of clever, obstreperous boy

indicators.note: knocking the stuffing out of each word empties its insides, leaving just the first and last letters of all three

explanation.surface: A singer is beating up an unruly, too-clever lad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking stuffing out of' keeps only the outer letters of each word: CR, OS and BY.
explanation.definitionFit: Bing Crosby was the hugely popular American crooner of White Christmas fame.

clue.text: Chesterton, perhaps, or the individual behind "Thursday"

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold, whose chemical symbol is Au
Thursday is named after Thor, the Norse god of thunder

explanation.surface: A question of whether Chesterton or someone else stands behind a thing called Thursday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' looks like a link but is gold in heraldry. The surface also nods to Chesterton's novel The Man Who Was Thursday, so the Norse god doubles as a hint at the book.
explanation.definitionFit: G K Chesterton was an English writer of novels and the Father Brown stories, an example of a novelist.

clue.text: Reasons Barking isn't Venice

indicators.note: barking means mad, so the letters of the words that follow go crazy into a new order

explanation.surface: An explanation of why Barking, an East London suburb, is not Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a suburb of East London, which makes it look like a place name; it is really the anagram signal, as in 'barking mad'.
explanation.definitionFit: Incentives are motives that encourage action, so they are reasons for doing something.

clue.text: Removing clothes here, Freda dropped a clanger

indicators.note: taking the clothes off each word strips away its outer letters, leaving the middle of both words

explanation.surface: Freda caused embarrassment by undressing in this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Removing clothes' strips the outer letters from both words: ER from 'here' and RED from 'Freda'.
explanation.definitionFit: To drop a clanger is a British idiom for making a blunder, so it means to have made a mistake.

clue.text: Bit backside of dim Conservative in contempt

indicators.note: the backside of a word is its rear end, so only its final letter is taken
in shows the Conservative letter going inside the word for contempt

parts.note: odium means hatred or contempt

explanation.surface: A slightly stupid Tory politician is being held in contempt of court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backside of' gives M, the last letter of 'dim'; 'in' puts C inside ODIUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A modicum is a small quantity, just a little bit of something.

clue.text: Promises made by politicians as I foment revolt

indicators.note: a revolt overturns things, so the letters of the preceding words are turned into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A rabble-rouser announces that the politicians' pledges are being used to stir up rebellion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolt' is the anagram signal acting on AS I FOMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A party's published programme of policy pledges before an election is called its manifesto.

clue.text: Chinless wonder departs with grave expression

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for departs, as on a timetable
RIP, rest in peace, is the phrase carved on a gravestone

explanation.surface: A feeble upper-class twit leaves looking solemn.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'chinless wonder' is British slang for a feeble, ineffectual (often upper-class) man. 'grave' here is the burial place, not the serious mood.
explanation.definitionFit: A drip is a weak, wet, spineless person, just like a chinless wonder.

clue.text: Chubby-faced, louche, rubicund host

indicators.note: the words act as host, holding the answer as a guest within their letters

explanation.surface: A dissolute, ruddy-faced landlord with a round face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'host' signals that 'louche, rubicund' holds the answer across the gap between the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Cherubs are pictured as plump-cheeked infants, so cherubic describes a round, innocent-looking face.

clue.text: One's about to cover race in Grauniad, supposedly

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second, covering it
about here means turned round, so the short form for one is is written backwards

parts.note: one's expands to one is, which from the speaker is I'm, giving IM
a sprint is a short fast race

explanation.surface: Someone is about to report on a race for the Guardian newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' expands to I'M, and 'about' turns it round; 'to cover' puts it on top in this down entry. Private Eye nicknamed the Guardian the Grauniad for its typing errors, so the nickname is itself one.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname is a deliberate scrambling of the paper's title, mocking its typos, so it is supposedly a printing error.

clue.text: Pensioner ignoring a twitching of the eye

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving out, so the letter a is dropped from the pensioner word

parts.note: OAP is old-age pensioner
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: An elderly person who pays no attention to a nervous flicker of the eyelid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring a' drops the A from OAP, leaving OP.
explanation.definitionFit: Optic is an adjective relating to sight or the eyes, as in the optic nerve.

clue.text: Weedy kid's condition worrying nit nurses

indicators.note: worrying means harrying or shaking about, so the letters of the words that follow are jumbled

explanation.surface: School nurses who check for head lice fret about a sickly child's health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nit nurses' were the school nurses who checked children's hair for lice; 'worrying' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A runt is the weakest, smallest of a litter, so the state of being a small, weedy child is runtiness.

clue.text: Bored Cockney geezer in dark shed

indicators.note: in puts the Cockney man between the two other pieces

parts.note: brown is a dark colour
to doff is to take off or shed, as a hat
he, a man, said by a Cockney dropping the H, becomes 'E

explanation.surface: A London lad is hiding in a gloomy garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys famously drop the H, so 'he' becomes 'E. 'shed' looks like a garden hut but is a verb, to take off.
explanation.definitionFit: Browned off is British slang for fed up or bored.

clue.text: Turn up car engine noise

indicators.note: turn tells us to flip the word that follows so it reads the other way

parts.note: RR is Rolls-Royce, a car

explanation.surface: Someone instructs a driver to rev their car's engine so it roars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn up' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'Turn' alone reverses the word 'up'. The car is a Rolls-Royce, abbreviated by its two initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoothly idling motor makes a low, contented hum like a cat, which is called a purr.

clue.text: Invalid setting off after lass, excited and tense

indicators.note: excited means stirred up, so the letters of the words before it are agitated into a new order

parts.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A sick person sets out in pursuit of a girl, aroused and nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invalid' reads as a sick person, but here it means not valid; 'excited' is the anagram signal on AFTER LASS.
explanation.definitionFit: In a race, a start that is not valid because a runner moved too early is a false start.

clue.text: Swarm of relaxed, fit Etonians

indicators.note: relaxed means loosened, so the letters of the words that follow are freed into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A crowd of easy-going, athletic schoolboys from Eton College.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is an elite English boarding school; 'relaxed' is the anagram signal on FIT ETONIANS.
explanation.definitionFit: An infestation is an invasion by a large number of pests, a swarm of them.

clue.text: Bloody huge birds

parts.note: flaming and bloody are both mild British swear words used as intensifiers
OS is the abbreviation for outsize, meaning huge

explanation.surface: An exclamation at some enormous birds.
explanation.walkthrough: OS stands for 'outsize', the British label for extra-large clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Flamingos are tall pink wading birds.

clue.text: Was SAS single-handedly apprehending killer?

indicators.note: apprehending means seizing hold of, so the words grab the answer within their letters

explanation.surface: A question of whether the special forces soldier captured the murderer alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apprehending' signals that the answer is held inside 'Was SAS single-handedly'. The SAS is the British Army's Special Air Service.
explanation.definitionFit: An assassin is a murderer, specifically one who kills a prominent person.

clue.text: French city state had money

indicators.note: state means say out loud, so the phrase it describes is heard rather than spelled

parts.note: bore dough: bore means carried or had, and dough is slang for money

explanation.surface: A French city that was once wealthy as a state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state' looks like a noun for a nation, but it is a verb meaning 'say'. BORE DOUGH (had money) said aloud gives the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Bordeaux is a major port city in south-west France, famous for its wine.

clue.text: The likes of Jude, single mother with kids on street

indicators.note: on places the single mother and kids upon the street, so the street abbreviation leads the build

parts.note: one means single
ma is mother
sons are children

explanation.surface: A single mum lives with her children on a street.
explanation.walkthrough: Jude Fawley, hero of Thomas Hardy's novel Jude the Obscure, is a stonecutter.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's Jude works as a stone-carver, so craftsmen like him are builders who dress and lay stone.

clue.text: Autobiographical scribblings of Arachne in sea at St Tropez?

indicators.note: in puts the setter's French self inside the French word for the sea

parts.note: mer is French for sea, and St Tropez is a resort on the French Riviera
Arachne is the setter, who would say me, or in French moi

explanation.surface: The setter's life story written while bathing off the French Riviera.
explanation.walkthrough: Arachne is the setter, so stands for 'me'; 'at St Tropez' makes both pieces French, and 'in' puts the setter inside the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A memoir is a written account of one's own life and experiences.

clue.text: Inhales aroma permeating smalls

indicators.note: permeating means spreading through, so the smell goes inside the letters for the underwear

parts.note: small is S, so smalls is two of them
niff is British slang for a smell

explanation.surface: Someone inhales a smell that has got into their underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smalls' is British slang for underwear, but here it is just S plus S; 'permeating' puts NIFF inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: To breathe in sharply through the nose is to sniff, so the verb forms match the clue's breathing in.

clue.text: Adjutant in theory moving closer to the front

indicators.note: the clue's closing letter is shifted nearer the start, moving the final letter of the word to the front

parts.note: an idea is a theory or notion

explanation.surface: An army officer is shifting closer to the battlefield, at least in theory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving closer to the front' moves the closing A of IDEA to the front. 'closer' means 'the last letter', not 'nearer'.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjutant is an officer who assists a commander, an assistant in other words.

clue.text: Support for labourers, if left back in Minnesota?

indicators.note: left means departed, so the letters of if go out of the word they sat in

parts.note: a midwife assists women in labour
the stern is the back of a ship

explanation.surface: A union's help for workers, if it left the back of the state of Minnesota.
explanation.walkthrough: 'labourers' are women in labour, not workers. 'if left' removes IF from MIDWIFE, leaving MIDWE.
explanation.definitionFit: Minnesota lies in the Midwest region of the US, so something there is of that region, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Well content with exchange rate

indicators.note: exchange means swap around, so the letters of the following word trade places

explanation.surface: Someone is quite happy with the currency exchange rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well content' looks like 'quite satisfied', but it means what a well contains; 'exchange' looks like part of 'exchange rate' but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A well is a shaft sunk to draw up liquid, and what it holds is the drink from underground.

clue.text: Voice of ballot box regularly ignored

indicators.note: every other letter is passed over at regular intervals, keeping the second, fourth and so on

explanation.surface: A voter's say in an election is routinely ignored at the ballot box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly ignored' drops alternate letters of 'ballot box', starting with the B.
explanation.definitionFit: An alto is a singing voice lower than soprano, so in music it is a type of voice.

clue.text: Sailor ringed by faint nocturnal shimmer

indicators.note: ringed by means surrounded, so the sailor is placed inside the word for faint

parts.note: slight means faint, as in a slight chance
tar is an old term for a sailor

explanation.surface: A seaman surrounded by a dim glimmer at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ringed by' puts the sailor inside the word for faint; tar is old slang for a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The faint glow of the stars twinkling in the night sky is starlight.

clue.text: Haughty female pursuing Murphy in Mumbai?

indicators.note: pursuing means coming after, so the female letter follows the potato word

parts.note: murphy is slang for a potato, and aloo is the word for potato in Indian cooking

explanation.surface: A snooty woman chasing a man called Murphy around Mumbai.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Murphy' looks like a surname but is old slang for a potato, an Irish staple; in Mumbai, an Indian city, that is ALOO, as in aloo gobi.
explanation.definitionFit: Aloof means distant and reserved, which comes across as haughty.

clue.text: Nasty Cameron's base promises to pay off debts

parts.note: as Prime Minister David Cameron lived at Number 10 Downing Street, written No X with the Roman numeral for ten
IOUs are written promises to repay, I owe you

explanation.surface: An unpleasant Prime Minister's power base pledges to pay off national debts.
explanation.walkthrough: David Cameron was UK Prime Minister, whose official home is Number 10 Downing Street: NO plus X, the Roman numeral for 10.
explanation.definitionFit: Noxious means harmful or poisonous, and so very unpleasant.

clue.text: Goes on ramble on vacation and comes back

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the goes piece comes after the rambling one
a word on vacation has emptied out, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: turns are goes, as in taking turns in a game

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker goes walking on a break, then heads home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on vacation' empties 'ramble' to its outer letters, and 'on' sets the word for goes after them.
explanation.definitionFit: To return is to come back to a place, so the verb forms match exactly.
